```python
CUTS = ("overall", "run", "pass", "early_down_run")


def attach_cut_columns(
    frame: pd.DataFrame,
    *,
    play_type_col: str,
    down_col: str,
    distance_col: str,
    gain_col: str,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Add _run_pass, _derived_success and _graded.

    The column names are arguments because this runs over two differently
    shaped frames: a raw CFBD season, and the joined Baylor table. What it
    must NOT do is take them from different sources on the two sides -- both
    callers pass CFBD columns, which is the whole point of the module.
    """
    out = frame.copy()
    out["_run_pass"] = out[play_type_col].map(classify_run_pass)
    out["_derived_success"] = [
        derive_success(down, distance, gain)
        for down, distance, gain in zip(
            out[down_col], out[distance_col], out[gain_col]
        )
    ]
    # Graded means gradeable: a real run or pass, on a down with a
    # convention. Penalties and fumble recoveries are plays but not grades.
    out["_graded"] = (
        out["_run_pass"].isin(("run", "pass"))
        & out["_derived_success"].notna()
    )
    return out


def apply_cut(frame: pd.DataFrame, cut: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One of CUTS. Assumes attach_cut_columns has run."""
    if cut == "overall":
        return frame
    if cut == "run":
        return frame[frame["_run_pass"] == "run"]
    if cut == "pass":
        return frame[frame["_run_pass"] == "pass"]
    if cut == "early_down_run":
        return frame[
            (frame["_run_pass"] == "run") & frame["_down_for_cut"].isin((1, 2))
        ]
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown cut {cut!r}. Known cuts: {', '.join(CUTS)}")


def flag_garbage(frame: pd.DataFrame, *, period_col: str = "period") -> pd.Series:
    """Garbage time from the PRE-snap score, never the post-play score."""
    margin = pd.to_numeric(
        frame["pre_offense_score"], errors="coerce"
    ) - pd.to_numeric(frame["pre_defense_score"], errors="coerce")
    return pd.Series(
        [
            epa.is_garbage_time(period, value)
            if pd.notna(period) and pd.notna(value)
            else False
            for period, value in zip(frame[period_col], margin)
        ],
        index=frame.index,
    )


def summarise(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
    """plays, graded, successes and the EPA (CFBD PPA) totals.

    plays, graded and epa_plays are three different counts and all three are
    returned. A play can be graded with no EPA (CFBD scores no penalty-wiped
    play) and can carry EPA without being graded (a fumble recovery). Using
    one as the other is how a coverage problem turns into a wrong rate.
    """
    values = pd.to_numeric(frame.get("_epa"), errors="coerce")
    graded = frame["_graded"]
    successes = int((graded & frame["_derived_success"].fillna(False)).sum())
    epa_plays = int(values.notna().sum())
    epa_total = float(values.sum()) if epa_plays else 0.0
    graded_n = int(graded.sum())

    return {
        "plays": int(len(frame)),
        "graded": graded_n,
        "successes": successes,
        "success_rate": round(successes / graded_n, 4) if graded_n else None,
        "epa_plays": epa_plays,
        "epa_total": round(epa_total, 4),
        "epa_per_play": round(epa_total / epa_plays, 4) if epa_plays else None,
    }


def defence_baseline(
    season_plays: pd.DataFrame,
    opponent_cfbd_name: str,
    cut: str,
    *,
    exclude_garbage: bool = False,
) -> dict:
    """What one defence allowed non-Baylor FBS offences, on one cut.

    Baylor is excluded by offence name, not by game, so a hypothetical second
    meeting in the same season is excluded too. Without that the adjustment is
    circular -- Baylor's own bad day would make the opponent look better,
    which would then partly excuse Baylor's bad day.
    """
    frame = season_plays[
        (season_plays["defense"] == opponent_cfbd_name)
        & (season_plays["offense"] != BAYLOR)
        & season_plays["offenseConference"].map(is_fbs)
    ].copy()

    frame = frame[~frame["playType"].map(epa.is_non_play)]

    frame = attach_cut_columns(
        frame,
        play_type_col="playType",
        down_col="down",
        distance_col="distance",
        gain_col="yardsGained",
    )
    frame["_down_for_cut"] = pd.to_numeric(frame["down"], errors="coerce")
    frame["_epa"] = pd.to_numeric(frame["ppa"], errors="coerce")

    if exclude_garbage:
        frame = frame[~flag_garbage(frame)]

    return summarise(apply_cut(frame, cut))
```

```python
def baylor_cut_frame(
    joined: pd.DataFrame,
    season: int,
    cut: str,
    *,
    exclude_garbage: bool = False,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Baylor's plays for one cut, classified the way the baseline is.

    Every classifying column here comes from CFBD, not the chart, and that is
    the point. The chart records the play CALL and CFBD records the RESULT;
    46 plays are charted P and typed Rush. A chart-classified Baylor rate
    subtracted from a CFBD-classified baseline would compare two different
    things and say nothing.

    down and distance are the chart's, and that is not an exception: they are
    the join key, so on a matched row they equal CFBD's by construction.
    """
    frame = joined[joined["season"] == season].copy()
    frame = attach_cut_columns(
        frame,
        play_type_col="cfbd_play_type",
        down_col="down",
        distance_col="distance",
        gain_col="cfbd_yards_gained",
    )
    frame["_down_for_cut"] = pd.to_numeric(frame["down"], errors="coerce")
    frame["_epa"] = pd.to_numeric(frame["epa"], errors="coerce")

    if exclude_garbage:
        frame = frame[~frame["garbage_time"].fillna(False).astype(bool)]

    return apply_cut(frame, cut)
```

```python
def schedule_strength(
    joined: pd.DataFrame,
    season_plays: pd.DataFrame,
    season: int,
    cut: str,
    *,
    exclude_garbage: bool = False,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One row per Baylor game: what Baylor did, and what that defence
    normally allowed.

    This is the descriptive answer on its own. If Baylor's 2025 opponents did
    not allow materially less than its 2024 opponents, opponent adjustment is
    refuted as the explanation before any subtraction is done.
    """
    baylor = baylor_cut_frame(
        joined, season, cut, exclude_garbage=exclude_garbage
    )

    rows = []
    for game_code, game in baylor.groupby("game_code", sort=True):
        code = game["def_team"].dropna().iloc[0]
        name = cfbd.OPPONENT_TO_CFBD[code]  # raises by name on an unmapped code

        conference = season_plays.loc[
            season_plays["defense"] == name, "defenseConference"
        ]
        level = opponent_level(
            conference.iloc[0] if len(conference) else None
        )

        baseline = defence_baseline(
            season_plays, name, cut, exclude_garbage=exclude_garbage
        )
        summary = summarise(game)

        rows.append({
            "season": season,
            "cut": cut,
            "game_code": game_code,
            "opponent": code,
            "opponent_cfbd": name,
            "level": level,
            "baylor_plays": summary["plays"],
            "baylor_graded": summary["graded"],
            "baylor_successes": summary["successes"],
            "baylor_epa_plays": summary["epa_plays"],
            "baylor_epa_total": summary["epa_total"],
            "baseline_plays": baseline["plays"],
            "baseline_graded": baseline["graded"],
            "baseline_epa_plays": baseline["epa_plays"],
            "baseline_epa_per_play": baseline["epa_per_play"],
            "baseline_success_rate": baseline["success_rate"],
```

```python
def _weighted(values, weights):
    """Play-weighted mean, skipping rows with no baseline.

    Weighted, not a mean of means: a 90-play game must not weigh the same as
    a 30-play game.
    """
    pairs = [
        (value, weight)
        for value, weight in zip(values, weights)
        if value is not None and pd.notna(value) and weight
    ]
    if not pairs:
        return None, 0
    total_weight = sum(weight for _, weight in pairs)
    return sum(value * weight for value, weight in pairs) / total_weight, total_weight


def adjusted_table(
    joined: pd.DataFrame,
    plays_by_season: dict[int, pd.DataFrame],
    cut: str,
    *,
    exclude_garbage: bool = False,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One row per season: raw, raw-FBS-only, baseline, adjusted.

    Three raw columns rather than one, because excluding the FCS game moves
    Baylor's RAW number too. A reader who saw only `adjusted` beside
    REPORT.md's 57.4% would reasonably conclude one document was wrong. The
    step from raw_all_games to raw_fbs_only is schedule composition; the step
    from there to adjusted is opponent quality.
    """
    rows = []
    for season in sorted(plays_by_season):
        games = schedule_strength(
            joined, plays_by_season[season], season, cut,
            exclude_garbage=exclude_garbage,
        )
        if games.empty:
            continue
        fbs = games[games["level"] == "fbs"]

        def ratio(frame, numerator, denominator):
            total = frame[denominator].sum()
            return round(frame[numerator].sum() / total, 4) if total else None

        baseline_epa, _ = _weighted(
            fbs["baseline_epa_per_play"], fbs["baylor_epa_plays"]
        )
        baseline_sr, _ = _weighted(
            fbs["baseline_success_rate"], fbs["baylor_graded"]
        )
        raw_fbs_epa = ratio(fbs, "baylor_epa_total", "baylor_epa_plays")
        raw_fbs_sr = ratio(fbs, "baylor_successes", "baylor_graded")

        rows.append({
            "season": season,
            "cut": cut,
            "games": int(len(games)),
            "games_fbs": int(len(fbs)),
            "plays": int(games["baylor_plays"].sum()),
            "graded": int(games["baylor_graded"].sum()),
            "epa_plays": int(games["baylor_epa_plays"].sum()),
            "raw_all_games_epa": ratio(games, "baylor_epa_total", "baylor_epa_plays"),
            "raw_fbs_only_epa": raw_fbs_epa,
            "schedule_baseline_epa": round(baseline_epa, 4) if baseline_epa is not None else None,
            "adjusted_epa": round(raw_fbs_epa - baseline_epa, 4)
                if raw_fbs_epa is not None and baseline_epa is not None else None,
            "raw_all_games_sr": ratio(games, "baylor_successes", "baylor_graded"),
            "raw_fbs_only_sr": raw_fbs_sr,
            "schedule_baseline_sr": round(baseline_sr, 4) if baseline_sr is not None else None,
            "adjusted_sr": round(raw_fbs_sr - baseline_sr, 4)
                if raw_fbs_sr is not None and baseline_sr is not None else None,
        })

    return pd.DataFrame(rows)
```

```python
def reconcile_success(joined: pd.DataFrame) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, dict]:
    """Baylor's charted Efficiency against the 50/70/100 convention.

    CLAUDE.md requires that a re-derived success flag be reconciled against
    the charted one and the disagreement rate published. This does that, and
    it is a finding in its own right: it says how far the staff's hand-tagged
    flag sits from the convention every public number uses.

    Chart fields on both sides, deliberately. The question is whether the
    charted flag agrees with the convention applied to the charted gain, not
    whether the chart agrees with CFBD -- that is a separate figure, in
    provenance.
    """
    frame = joined.copy()
    graded = ~frame["efficiency"].isin(SUCCESS_RATE_EXCLUDED)
    frame = frame[graded].copy()

    frame["_charted"] = frame["efficiency"].eq("Y")
    frame["_derived"] = [
        derive_success(down, distance, gain)
        for down, distance, gain in zip(
            frame["down"], frame["distance"], frame["gain"]
        )
    ]
    frame = frame[frame["_derived"].notna()].copy()
    frame["_derived"] = frame["_derived"].astype(bool)

    crosstab = (
        frame.groupby(["season", "_charted", "_derived"])
        .size()
        .reset_index(name="plays")
    )

    agree = int((frame["_charted"] == frame["_derived"]).sum())
    compared = int(len(frame))
    summary = {
        "compared": compared,
        "agreement_rate": round(agree / compared, 4) if compared else None,
        "charted_only": int((frame["_charted"] & ~frame["_derived"]).sum()),
        "derived_only": int((~frame["_charted"] & frame["_derived"]).sum()),
    }
    return crosstab, summary
```

```python
"""Phase 5: what Baylor's schedule allowed everyone else.

Phase 4 showed the 2024-to-2025 decline is not explained by alignment. The
strongest remaining structural explanation is the schedule: 2025 defences may
simply have been better. This module measures that.

Everything here classifies plays from CFBD's own columns rather than from
Baylor's charting file, and the reason is not convenience. There is no chart
for an opponent's other games, so a baseline can only be built from CFBD. A
Baylor rate built from the chart and subtracted from a baseline built from
CFBD would compare two different things -- the chart records the play CALL,
CFBD records the RESULT, and they disagree on 46 scrambles charted P and typed
Rush. So both sides of every subtraction are classified the same way, here.

Read-only against CFB_Analytics_Lab's parquet. Never calls the CFBD API.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import pandas as pd

BAYLOR = "Baylor"

# CFBD's own conference strings, read from the parquet rather than assumed.
# CFBD writes "American Athletic", not "AAC", and "Mid-American", not "MAC".
FBS_CONFERENCES = frozenset({
    "ACC",
    "American Athletic",
    "Big 12",
    "Big Ten",
    "Conference USA",
    "FBS Independents",
    "Mid-American",
    "Mountain West",
    "Pac-12",
    "SEC",
    "Sun Belt",
})

# Only the FCS conferences an opponent could plausibly come from. This exists
# to make opponent_level raise on anything it does not recognise, so a
# realignment fails by name instead of quietly demoting a team out of the
# headline. It is not used to filter baseline offences -- is_fbs does that,
# and a Division II offence is simply not FBS.
FCS_CONFERENCES = frozenset({
    "Big Sky",
    "Coastal Athletic",
    "FCS Independents",
    "Ivy",
    "MEAC",
    "MVFC",
    "NEC",
    "OVC-Big South",
    "Patriot",
    "Pioneer",
    "SWAC",
    "Southern",
    "Southland",
    "UAC",
})

# CFBD play type -> run / pass. Explicit, and deliberately partial.
#
# Everything absent resolves to "unknown", which is excluded from run and pass
# cuts on BOTH sides of every subtraction. Fumble recoveries are the reason
# this is not a two-way split: CFBD gives them their own play type and never
# says whether the snap behind them was a run or a pass. Defaulting them to
# either would bias that cut, and they are 0.6% of plays.
#
# Penalty is here as "unknown" for a second reason. A CFBD penalty row carries
# a down, a distance and a yardsGained, so a derived success flag would score
# every penalty as a failure. Mapping it to unknown keeps it in the play pool
# -- where this repo wants it -- while keeping it out of every graded
# denominator.
CFBD_PLAY_TYPE_TO_RUN_PASS = {
    "Rush": "run",
    "Rushing Touchdown": "run",
    "Pass Reception": "pass",
    "Pass Incompletion": "pass",
    "Pass Completion": "pass",
    "Passing Touchdown": "pass",
    "Sack": "pass",
    "Interception": "pass",
    "Pass Interception Return": "pass",
    "Interception Return Touchdown": "pass",
}

UNKNOWN = "unknown"

# Down -> the share of the distance a play must gain to succeed. The standard
# convention, the same one nflfastR and Football Outsiders use. Baylor's chart
# carries its own hand-tagged Efficiency flag; the two are reconciled and the
# disagreement rate published rather than one being assumed to equal the other.
_SUCCESS_THRESHOLD = {1: 0.5, 2: 0.7, 3: 1.0, 4: 1.0}


def classify_run_pass(play_type) -> str:
    """"run", "pass", or "unknown". Never guesses."""
    if not isinstance(play_type, str):
        return UNKNOWN
    return CFBD_PLAY_TYPE_TO_RUN_PASS.get(play_type, UNKNOWN)


def derive_success(down, distance, gain) -> bool | None:
    """The 50 / 70 / 100 convention. None when the play cannot be graded.

    None rather than False for an ungradeable play, because a fifth down is
    not a failed play -- it is a play with no convention. Returning False
    would put it in the denominator as a stop.
    """
    if pd.isna(down) or pd.isna(distance) or pd.isna(gain):
        return None
    threshold = _SUCCESS_THRESHOLD.get(int(down))
    if threshold is None:
        return None
    return float(gain) >= threshold * float(distance)


def is_fbs(conference) -> bool:
    """Total, and never raises. A Division II offence is simply not FBS."""
    return conference in FBS_CONFERENCES


def opponent_level(conference) -> str:
    """"fbs" or "fcs" for one of Baylor's opponents. Raises on anything else.

    Deliberately not total. This is called only on teams Baylor actually
    played, where an unrecognised conference means a realignment or a CFBD
    rename -- and quietly returning "fcs" would drop a real conference game
    out of the headline without a word.
    """
    if conference in FBS_CONFERENCES:
        return "fbs"
    if conference in FCS_CONFERENCES:
        return "fcs"
    raise ValueError(
        f"Unknown conference {conference!r}. Add it to FBS_CONFERENCES or "
        "FCS_CONFERENCES in src/playcalls/opponent.py. It is not guessed, "
        "because guessing 'fcs' would drop the game from the headline."
    )
```

```python
def load_season_plays(
    season: int, root: str = cfbd.CFBD_PLAYS_ROOT

    cfbd.load_baylor_plays filters to one offence in SQL. This does not,

    why cfbd._attach_pre_snap_score had to be grouped by (game, offence):
```

```python
CUTS = ("overall", "run", "pass", "early_down_run")


def attach_cut_columns(
    frame: pd.DataFrame,
    *,
    play_type_col: str,
    down_col: str,
    distance_col: str,
    gain_col: str,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Add _run_pass, _derived_success and _graded.

    The column names are arguments because this runs over two differently
    shaped frames: a raw CFBD season, and the joined Baylor table. What it
    must NOT do is take them from different sources on the two sides -- both
    callers pass CFBD columns, which is the whole point of the module.
    """
    out = frame.copy()
    out["_run_pass"] = out[play_type_col].map(classify_run_pass)
    out["_derived_success"] = [
        derive_success(down, distance, gain)
        for down, distance, gain in zip(
            out[down_col], out[distance_col], out[gain_col]
        )
    ]
    # Graded means gradeable: a real run or pass, on a down with a
    # convention. Penalties and fumble recoveries are plays but not grades.
    out["_graded"] = (
        out["_run_pass"].isin(("run", "pass"))
        & out["_derived_success"].notna()
    )
    return out


def apply_cut(frame: pd.DataFrame, cut: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One of CUTS. Assumes attach_cut_columns has run."""
    if cut == "overall":
        return frame
    if cut == "run":
        return frame[frame["_run_pass"] == "run"]
    if cut == "pass":
        return frame[frame["_run_pass"] == "pass"]
    if cut == "early_down_run":
        return frame[
            (frame["_run_pass"] == "run") & frame["_down_for_cut"].isin((1, 2))
        ]
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown cut {cut!r}. Known cuts: {', '.join(CUTS)}")


def flag_garbage(frame: pd.DataFrame, *, period_col: str = "period") -> pd.Series:
    """Garbage time from the PRE-snap score, never the post-play score."""
    margin = pd.to_numeric(
        frame["pre_offense_score"], errors="coerce"
    ) - pd.to_numeric(frame["pre_defense_score"], errors="coerce")
    return pd.Series(
        [
            epa.is_garbage_time(period, value)
            if pd.notna(period) and pd.notna(value)
            else False
            for period, value in zip(frame[period_col], margin)
        ],
        index=frame.index,
    )


def summarise(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
    """plays, graded, successes and the EPA (CFBD PPA) totals.

    plays, graded and epa_plays are three different counts and all three are
    returned. A play can be graded with no EPA (CFBD scores no penalty-wiped
    play) and can carry EPA without being graded (a fumble recovery). Using
    one as the other is how a coverage problem turns into a wrong rate.
    """
    values = pd.to_numeric(frame.get("_epa"), errors="coerce")
    graded = frame["_graded"]
    successes = int((graded & frame["_derived_success"].fillna(False)).sum())
    epa_plays = int(values.notna().sum())
    epa_total = float(values.sum()) if epa_plays else 0.0
    graded_n = int(graded.sum())

    return {
        "plays": int(len(frame)),
        "graded": graded_n,
        "successes": successes,
        "success_rate": round(successes / graded_n, 4) if graded_n else None,
        "epa_plays": epa_plays,
        "epa_total": round(epa_total, 4),
        "epa_per_play": round(epa_total / epa_plays, 4) if epa_plays else None,
    }


def defence_baseline(
    season_plays: pd.DataFrame,
    opponent_cfbd_name: str,
    cut: str,
    *,
    exclude_garbage: bool = False,
) -> dict:
    """What one defence allowed non-Baylor FBS offences, on one cut.

    Baylor is excluded by offence name, not by game, so a hypothetical second
    meeting in the same season is excluded too. Without that the adjustment is
    circular -- Baylor's own bad day would make the opponent look better,
    which would then partly excuse Baylor's bad day.
    """
    frame = season_plays[
        (season_plays["defense"] == opponent_cfbd_name)
        & (season_plays["offense"] != BAYLOR)
        & season_plays["offenseConference"].map(is_fbs)
    ].copy()

    frame = frame[~frame["playType"].map(epa.is_non_play)]

    frame = attach_cut_columns(
        frame,
        play_type_col="playType",
        down_col="down",
        distance_col="distance",
        gain_col="yardsGained",
    )
    frame["_down_for_cut"] = pd.to_numeric(frame["down"], errors="coerce")
    frame["_epa"] = pd.to_numeric(frame["ppa"], errors="coerce")

    if exclude_garbage:
        frame = frame[~flag_garbage(frame)]

    return summarise(apply_cut(frame, cut))
```

```python
def baylor_cut_frame(
    joined: pd.DataFrame,
    season: int,
    cut: str,
    *,
    exclude_garbage: bool = False,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Baylor's plays for one cut, classified the way the baseline is.

    Every classifying column here comes from CFBD, not the chart, and that is
    the point. The chart records the play CALL and CFBD records the RESULT;
    46 plays are charted P and typed Rush. A chart-classified Baylor rate
    subtracted from a CFBD-classified baseline would compare two different
    things and say nothing.

    down and distance are the chart's, and that is not an exception: they are
    the join key, so on a matched row they equal CFBD's by construction.
    """
    frame = joined[joined["season"] == season].copy()
    frame = attach_cut_columns(
        frame,
        play_type_col="cfbd_play_type",
        down_col="down",
        distance_col="distance",
        gain_col="cfbd_yards_gained",
    )
    frame["_down_for_cut"] = pd.to_numeric(frame["down"], errors="coerce")
    frame["_epa"] = pd.to_numeric(frame["epa"], errors="coerce")

    if exclude_garbage:
        frame = frame[~frame["garbage_time"].fillna(False).astype(bool)]

    return apply_cut(frame, cut)
```

```python
def schedule_strength(
    joined: pd.DataFrame,
    season_plays: pd.DataFrame,
    season: int,
    cut: str,
    *,
    exclude_garbage: bool = False,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One row per Baylor game: what Baylor did, and what that defence
    normally allowed.

    This is the descriptive answer on its own. If Baylor's 2025 opponents did
    not allow materially less than its 2024 opponents, opponent adjustment is
    refuted as the explanation before any subtraction is done.
    """
    baylor = baylor_cut_frame(
        joined, season, cut, exclude_garbage=exclude_garbage
    )

    rows = []
    for game_code, game in baylor.groupby("game_code", sort=True):
        code = game["def_team"].dropna().iloc[0]
        name = cfbd.OPPONENT_TO_CFBD[code]  # raises by name on an unmapped code

        conference = season_plays.loc[
            season_plays["defense"] == name, "defenseConference"
        ]
        level = opponent_level(
            conference.iloc[0] if len(conference) else None
        )

        baseline = defence_baseline(
            season_plays, name, cut, exclude_garbage=exclude_garbage
        )
        summary = summarise(game)

        rows.append({
            "season": season,
            "cut": cut,
            "game_code": game_code,
            "opponent": code,
            "opponent_cfbd": name,
            "level": level,
            "baylor_plays": summary["plays"],
            "baylor_graded": summary["graded"],
            "baylor_successes": summary["successes"],
            "baylor_epa_plays": summary["epa_plays"],
            "baylor_epa_total": summary["epa_total"],
            "baseline_plays": baseline["plays"],
            "baseline_graded": baseline["graded"],
            "baseline_epa_plays": baseline["epa_plays"],
            "baseline_epa_per_play": baseline["epa_per_play"],
            "baseline_success_rate": baseline["success_rate"],
        })

    return pd.DataFrame(rows)
```

```python
def _weighted(values, weights):
    """Play-weighted mean, skipping rows with no baseline.

    Weighted, not a mean of means: a 90-play game must not weigh the same as
    a 30-play game.
    """
    pairs = [
        (value, weight)
        for value, weight in zip(values, weights)
        if value is not None and pd.notna(value) and weight
    ]
    if not pairs:
        return None, 0
    total_weight = sum(weight for _, weight in pairs)
    return sum(value * weight for value, weight in pairs) / total_weight, total_weight


def adjusted_table(
    joined: pd.DataFrame,
    plays_by_season: dict[int, pd.DataFrame],
    cut: str,
    *,
    exclude_garbage: bool = False,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One row per season: raw, raw-FBS-only, baseline, adjusted.

    Three raw columns rather than one, because excluding the FCS game moves
    Baylor's RAW number too. A reader who saw only `adjusted` beside
    REPORT.md's 57.4% would reasonably conclude one document was wrong. The
    step from raw_all_games to raw_fbs_only is schedule composition; the step
    from there to adjusted is opponent quality.
    """
    rows = []
    for season in sorted(plays_by_season):
        games = schedule_strength(
            joined, plays_by_season[season], season, cut,
            exclude_garbage=exclude_garbage,
        )
        if games.empty:
            continue
        fbs = games[games["level"] == "fbs"]

        def ratio(frame, numerator, denominator):
            total = frame[denominator].sum()
            return round(frame[numerator].sum() / total, 4) if total else None

        baseline_epa, _ = _weighted(
            fbs["baseline_epa_per_play"], fbs["baylor_epa_plays"]
        )
        baseline_sr, _ = _weighted(
            fbs["baseline_success_rate"], fbs["baylor_graded"]
        )
        raw_fbs_epa = ratio(fbs, "baylor_epa_total", "baylor_epa_plays")
```

```python
def reconcile_success(joined: pd.DataFrame) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, dict]:
    """Baylor's charted Efficiency against the 50/70/100 convention.

    CLAUDE.md requires that a re-derived success flag be reconciled against
    the charted one and the disagreement rate published. This does that, and
    it is a finding in its own right: it says how far the staff's hand-tagged
    flag sits from the convention every public number uses.

    Chart fields on both sides, deliberately. The question is whether the
    charted flag agrees with the convention applied to the charted gain, not
    whether the chart agrees with CFBD -- that is a separate figure, in
    provenance.
    """
    frame = joined.copy()
    graded = ~frame["efficiency"].isin(SUCCESS_RATE_EXCLUDED)
    frame = frame[graded].copy()

    frame["_charted"] = frame["efficiency"].eq("Y")
    frame["_derived"] = [
        derive_success(down, distance, gain)
        for down, distance, gain in zip(
            frame["down"], frame["distance"], frame["gain"]
        )
    ]
    frame = frame[frame["_derived"].notna()].copy()
    frame["_derived"] = frame["_derived"].astype(bool)

    crosstab = (
        frame.groupby(["season", "_charted", "_derived"])
        .size()
        .reset_index(name="plays")
    )

    agree = int((frame["_charted"] == frame["_derived"]).sum())
    compared = int(len(frame))
    summary = {
        "compared": compared,
        "agreement_rate": round(agree / compared, 4) if compared else None,
        "charted_only": int((frame["_charted"] & ~frame["_derived"]).sum()),
        "derived_only": int((~frame["_charted"] & frame["_derived"]).sum()),
    }
    return crosstab, summary
```

Import `SUCCESS_RATE_EXCLUDED` from `src.playcalls.charting`.

    """The all-teams defect. Grouping by gameId alone makes the previous

    def test_it_does_not_leak_across_offences_in_one_game(self):
        """The all-teams defect. Grouping by gameId alone makes the previous
        row's offenseScore belong to the OTHER team.

        One game, two possessions. Alpha scores a touchdown to go 7-0, then
        Beta takes over. Beta's first snap must read pre_offense_score 0 --
        Beta has not scored -- and pre_defense_score 7, because Alpha has.
        Grouping by gameId alone reads the previous row, Alpha's 7, as
        Beta's own score.

        load_baylor_plays filters to one offence in SQL, so this could never
        happen there. opponent.load_season_plays does not, because a
        defensive baseline needs the opponent's other games.
        """
        frame = pd.DataFrame({
            "gameId": [1, 1, 1, 1],
            "driveNumber": [1, 1, 2, 2],
            "playNumber": [1, 2, 1, 2],
            "offense": ["Alpha", "Alpha", "Beta", "Beta"],
            "defense": ["Beta", "Beta", "Alpha", "Alpha"],
            # Post-play scores, from each row's own offence's perspective.
            "offenseScore": [0, 7, 0, 0],
            "defenseScore": [0, 0, 7, 7],
        })

        out = cfbd._attach_pre_snap_score(frame)
        beta = out[out["offense"] == "Beta"].reset_index(drop=True)

        assert list(beta["pre_offense_score"]) == [0, 0], (
            "Beta's own score leaked from Alpha's row"
        )
        assert list(beta["pre_defense_score"]) == [7, 7], (

        grouping by (gameId, offense) yields identical groups to grouping by
        gameId. Asserted rather than assumed, because Phase 2's whole
        score-state analysis rests on these two columns.

"""CFBD loader and game map.

The game map is the highest-risk piece in Phase 2. CFBD labels Baylor's 2024
LSU bowl as seasonType=postseason week=1, so ordering games by week puts it
second rather than last. A positional map would misjoin the entire season and
every EPA number after it. These tests exist to make that impossible.

import pytest

def _chart(codes_and_opponents):
    return pd.DataFrame(
        [{"game_code": c, "def_team": o} for c, o in codes_and_opponents]
    )


def _cfbd(rows):
    return pd.DataFrame(
        [{"gameId": g, "defense": d, "week": w, "seasonType": s}
         for g, d, w, s in rows]
    )

    codes = ["TXTA", "UTUN", "COAF", "COUN", "UTBY", "IAST", "TXTC",

        assert code in cfbd.OPPONENT_TO_CFBD

ordered = frame.sort_values(
        ["gameId", "driveNumber", "playNumber"]
    ).reset_index(drop=True)

    # The score is tracked per TEAM, not per row perspective.
    #
    # offenseScore and defenseScore mean different teams on different rows,
    # because the offence changes hands. Shifting them directly is correct
    # only for a frame already filtered to one offence, which
    # load_baylor_plays produces in SQL and opponent.load_season_plays
    # deliberately does not -- a defensive baseline needs the opponent's
    # other games.
    #
    # So each row's two scores are first re-expressed against a fixed pair of
    # slots. The slots are ordered by team name, which is stable within a
    # game because every row of a game names the same two teams. After the
    # shift they are mapped back to the row's own perspective.
    #
    # For a single-offence frame the slot assignment is constant within each
    # game, so this reduces exactly to the previous groupby("gameId") shift
    # and every Phase 2 number is unchanged. A test asserts that.
    first_team = ordered[["offense", "defense"]].apply(min, axis=1)
    offence_is_first = ordered["offense"].eq(first_team)

    ordered["_score_first"] = ordered["offenseScore"].where(
        offence_is_first, ordered["defenseScore"]
    )
    ordered["_score_second"] = ordered["defenseScore"].where(
        offence_is_first, ordered["offenseScore"]
    )

    grouped = ordered.groupby("gameId", sort=False)
    pre_first = grouped["_score_first"].shift(1).fillna(0)
    pre_second = grouped["_score_second"].shift(1).fillna(0)

    pre_offense = pre_first.where(offence_is_first, pre_second)
    pre_defense = pre_second.where(offence_is_first, pre_first)

    ordered["pre_offense_score"] = (
        pre_offense.clip(upper=ordered["offenseScore"]).astype(int)
    )
    ordered["pre_defense_score"] = (
        pre_defense.clip(upper=ordered["defenseScore"]).astype(int)
    )

    return ordered.drop(columns=["_score_first", "_score_second"])

"""Read CFBD play-by-play, read-only.

CFB_Analytics_Lab owns all CFBD ingest. This module opens its parquet output
and nothing else. It never calls the CFBD API, never reads that repo's .env,
and holds no credential. If a season's parquet is absent, it raises with the
command to run over there rather than fetching, because the free tier is 1,000
calls a month and the budget guard and call ledger both live in that repo.

Games are mapped to chart game codes by opponent, never by week order. CFBD
labels Baylor's 2024 LSU bowl seasonType=postseason week=1, so ordering by week
places it second in the season instead of thirteenth. A positional map would
misjoin all of 2024 without erroring.

The `ppa` column is CFBD's Predicted Points Added, which is their name for EPA.
That was verified rather than assumed -- see the Phase 2 spec, section 2.2. In
short: CFBD's glossary defines it as their EPA measure over a multinomial
next-score model, and it reconciles as a change in expected points. Summed over
2024 drives starting near the own 25 it totals +5.09 on touchdown drives, +2.00
on field-goal drives and -0.80 on punts, against EPA theory of roughly +5.5,
+1.8 and -1.4. A yards proxy would not reconcile to points at all.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import pathlib

import duckdb
import pandas as pd

CFBD_PLAYS_ROOT = "/Users/kristinarash/DEV/CFB_Analytics_Lab/data/raw/plays"

# Chart / PFF four-character opponent code -> CFBD team name.
# Explicit by design. Derivation from the code's letters is not reliable:
# TXTA is Tarleton State, TXTC is Texas Tech, TXCU is TCU, TXMU is SMU.
OPPONENT_TO_CFBD = {
    # 2024
    "TXTA": "Tarleton State",
    "UTUN": "Utah",
    "COAF": "Air Force",
    "COUN": "Colorado",
    "UTBY": "BYU",
    "IAST": "Iowa State",
    "TXTC": "Texas Tech",
    "OKST": "Oklahoma State",
    "TXCU": "TCU",
    "WVUN": "West Virginia",
    "TXHO": "Houston",
    "KSUN": "Kansas",
    "LAST": "LSU",

misjoin all of 2024 without erroring.

short: CFBD's glossary defines it as their EPA measure over a multinomial

2024 drives starting near the own 25 it totals +5.09 on touchdown drives, +2.00

Carry the pre-snap score per team, not per row perspective

_attach_pre_snap_score shifted offenseScore and defenseScore directly
within a gameId group. That is correct only because load_baylor_plays
filters offense = 'Baylor' in SQL first, so every surviving row of a game
shares one offence and offenseScore always names the same team.

Phase 5 loads all teams. There the offence changes hands inside a game, so
offenseScore names a different team on different rows and shifting it reads
the OTHER team's score as this team's previous score. Nothing raises. Every
garbage-time flag and every score-state bucket built on it would simply be
wrong, which is the same class of defect as the post-play-score trap this
function already exists to fix.

The plan proposed regrouping by (gameId, offense). Building it showed that
is not enough: it restarts each team's series at 0-0, so a team taking over
after the opponent scored reads its opponent at zero. The fix has to track
both teams through the possession change.

Each row's two scores are re-expressed against a fixed pair of slots ordered
by team name -- stable within a game, because every row of a game names the
same two teams -- then shifted, then mapped back to the row's own
perspective. The clamp to the post-play score is unchanged and still carries
the unreliable-ordering protection.

For a single-offence frame the slot assignment is constant within each game,
so this reduces exactly to the previous shift. Asserted, not assumed: the
2024 and 2025 pre-snap columns hash identically before and after.

"""Phase 5: what Baylor's schedule allowed everyone else.

Phase 4 showed the 2024-to-2025 decline is not explained by alignment. Baylor
lined up the same, defences lined up the same, and the same concepts produced
less. The strongest remaining structural explanation is the schedule: 2025
defences may simply have been better. This module measures that.

Everything here classifies plays from CFBD's own columns rather than from
Baylor's charting file, and the reason is not convenience. There is no chart
for an opponent's other games, so a baseline can only be built from CFBD. The
chart records the play CALL and CFBD records the RESULT, and they disagree on
real plays -- 46 are charted `P` and typed `Rush`, which are scrambles. A
Baylor rate classified from the chart, subtracted from a baseline classified
from CFBD, would compare two different things and say nothing. So both sides
of every subtraction are classified the same way, here.

Read-only against CFB_Analytics_Lab's parquet. Never calls the CFBD API.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import pathlib

import duckdb
import pandas as pd

from src.playcalls import cfbd, epa
from src.playcalls.analysis import MIN_SAMPLE
from src.playcalls.charting import SUCCESS_RATE_EXCLUDED

BAYLOR = "Baylor"

# CFBD's own conference strings, read from the parquet rather than assumed.
# CFBD writes "American Athletic", not "AAC", and "Mid-American", not "MAC".
FBS_CONFERENCES = frozenset({
    "ACC",
    "American Athletic",
    "Big 12",
    "Big Ten",
    "Conference USA",
    "FBS Independents",
    "Mid-American",
    "Mountain West",
    "Pac-12",
    "SEC",
    "Sun Belt",
})

# Only the FCS conferences an opponent could plausibly come from. This exists
# so opponent_level raises on anything it does not recognise, which makes a
# realignment or a CFBD rename fail by name instead of quietly demoting a team
# out of the headline. It is NOT used to filter baseline offences -- is_fbs
# does that, and a Division II offence is simply not FBS.
FCS_CONFERENCES = frozenset({
    "Big Sky",
    "Coastal Athletic",
    "FCS Independents",
    "Ivy",
    "MEAC",
    "MVFC",
    "NEC",
    "OVC-Big South",
    "Patriot",
    "Pioneer",
    "SWAC",
    "Southern",
    "Southland",
    "UAC",
})

UNKNOWN = "unknown"

# CFBD play type -> run / pass. Explicit, and deliberately partial.
#
# Everything absent resolves to UNKNOWN, which is excluded from run and pass
# cuts on BOTH sides of every subtraction. Fumble recoveries are why this is
# not a two-way split: CFBD gives them their own play type and never says
# whether the snap behind them was a run or a pass. Defaulting them to either
# would bias that cut, and they are about 0.6% of plays.
#
# Penalty is UNKNOWN for a second reason. A CFBD penalty row carries a down, a
# distance and a yardsGained, so a derived success flag would score every
# penalty as a failure. UNKNOWN keeps it in the play pool -- where this repo
# wants it, because a wiped charting play genuinely corresponds to one -- while
# keeping it out of every graded denominator.
CFBD_PLAY_TYPE_TO_RUN_PASS = {
    "Rush": "run",
    "Rushing Touchdown": "run",
    "Pass Reception": "pass",
    "Pass Incompletion": "pass",
    "Pass Completion": "pass",
    "Passing Touchdown": "pass",
    "Sack": "pass",
    "Interception": "pass",
    "Pass Interception Return": "pass",
    "Interception Return Touchdown": "pass",
}

# Down -> the share of the distance a play must gain to succeed. The standard
# convention, the same one nflfastR and Football Outsiders use. Baylor's chart
# carries its own hand-tagged Efficiency flag; the two are reconciled by
# reconcile_success and the disagreement rate published, rather than one being
# assumed to equal the other.
_SUCCESS_THRESHOLD = {1: 0.5, 2: 0.7, 3: 1.0, 4: 1.0}

CUTS = ("overall", "run", "pass", "early_down_run")


def classify_run_pass(play_type) -> str:
    """"run", "pass", or "unknown". Never guesses."""
    if not isinstance(play_type, str):
        return UNKNOWN
    return CFBD_PLAY_TYPE_TO_RUN_PASS.get(play_type, UNKNOWN)


def derive_success(down, distance, gain) -> bool | None:
    """The 50 / 70 / 100 convention. None when the play cannot be graded.

    None rather than False for an ungradeable play. A fifth down is not a
    failed play; it is a play with no convention. Returning False would put it
    in the denominator as a stop.
    """
    if pd.isna(down) or pd.isna(distance) or pd.isna(gain):
        return None
    threshold = _SUCCESS_THRESHOLD.get(int(down))
    if threshold is None:
        return None
    return float(gain) >= threshold * float(distance)


def is_fbs(conference) -> bool:
    """Total, and never raises. A Division II offence is simply not FBS."""
    return conference in FBS_CONFERENCES


def opponent_level(conference) -> str:
    """"fbs" or "fcs" for one of Baylor's opponents. Raises on anything else.

    Deliberately not total. This is called only on teams Baylor actually
    played, where an unrecognised conference means a realignment or a CFBD
    rename -- and quietly returning "fcs" would drop a real conference game out
    of the headline without a word.
    """
    if conference in FBS_CONFERENCES:
        return "fbs"
    if conference in FCS_CONFERENCES:
        return "fcs"
    raise ValueError(
        f"Unknown conference {conference!r}. Add it to FBS_CONFERENCES or "
        "FCS_CONFERENCES in src/playcalls/opponent.py. It is not guessed, "
        "because guessing 'fcs' would drop the game from the headline."
    )


_SEASON_QUERY = """
select
    season,
    gameId,
    week,
    seasonType,
    offense,
    offenseConference,
    defense,
    defenseConference,
    period,
    down,
    distance,
    yardsToGoal,
    yardsGained,
    "clock.minutes" * 60 + "clock.seconds" as clock_rem,
    playType,
    ppa,
    offenseScore,
    defenseScore,
    driveNumber,
    playNumber
from read_parquet(?, union_by_name = true)
"""


def load_season_plays(
    season: int, root: str = cfbd.CFBD_PLAYS_ROOT
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Every play in one CFBD season, all teams.

    cfbd.load_baylor_plays filters to one offence in SQL. This does not,
    because a defensive baseline needs the opponent's OTHER games. That is
    exactly why cfbd._attach_pre_snap_score had to carry the score per team
    rather than per row perspective: in this frame the offence changes hands
    inside a game.

    The season is baked into the glob rather than filtered afterwards, for the
    same reason as load_baylor_plays -- Baylor plays Auburn in 2025 and again
    in 2026, and a cross-season glob would let one join the other's rows.
    """
    directory = pathlib.Path(root) / f"season={season}"
    if not directory.is_dir() or not list(directory.glob("*.parquet")):
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"No CFBD plays for {season} at {directory}.\n"
            "This repo never calls the CFBD API. Pull it in the repo that "
            "owns CFBD ingest, which enforces the free-tier budget guard:\n"
            f"  cd ~/DEV/CFB_Analytics_Lab && "
            f".venv/bin/python -m cfblab.pull plays --season {season}"
        )

    connection = duckdb.connect()
    try:
        frame = connection.execute(
            _SEASON_QUERY, [str(directory / "*.parquet")]
        ).df()
    finally:
        connection.close()

    frame["season"] = frame["season"].astype(int)
    return cfbd._attach_pre_snap_score(frame)


def attach_cut_columns(
    frame: pd.DataFrame,
    *,
    play_type_col: str,
    down_col: str,
    distance_col: str,
    gain_col: str,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Add _run_pass, _derived_success and _graded.

    The column names are arguments because this runs over two differently
    shaped frames: a raw CFBD season, and the joined Baylor table. What it must
    never do is take them from different SOURCES on the two sides -- both
    callers pass CFBD-derived columns, which is the whole point of the module.
    """
    out = frame.copy()
    out["_run_pass"] = out[play_type_col].map(classify_run_pass)
    out["_derived_success"] = [
        derive_success(down, distance, gain)
        for down, distance, gain in zip(
            out[down_col], out[distance_col], out[gain_col]
        )
    ]
    # Graded means gradeable: a real run or pass, on a down that has a
    # convention. Penalties and fumble recoveries are plays but not grades.
    out["_graded"] = (
        out["_run_pass"].isin(("run", "pass"))
        & out["_derived_success"].notna()
    )
    return out


def apply_cut(frame: pd.DataFrame, cut: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One of CUTS. Assumes attach_cut_columns and _down_for_cut have run."""
    if cut == "overall":
        return frame
    if cut == "run":
        return frame[frame["_run_pass"] == "run"]
    if cut == "pass":
        return frame[frame["_run_pass"] == "pass"]
    if cut == "early_down_run":
        return frame[
            (frame["_run_pass"] == "run") & frame["_down_for_cut"].isin((1, 2))
        ]
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown cut {cut!r}. Known cuts: {', '.join(CUTS)}")


def flag_garbage(frame: pd.DataFrame, *, period_col: str = "period") -> pd.Series:
    """Garbage time from the PRE-snap score, never the post-play score."""
    offense = pd.to_numeric(frame["pre_offense_score"], errors="coerce")
    defense = pd.to_numeric(frame["pre_defense_score"], errors="coerce")
    margin = offense - defense
    return pd.Series(
        [
            epa.is_garbage_time(period, value)
            if pd.notna(period) and pd.notna(value)
            else False
            for period, value in zip(frame[period_col], margin)
        ],
        index=frame.index,
    )


def summarise(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
    """plays, graded, successes and the EPA (CFBD PPA) totals.

    plays, graded and epa_plays are three different counts and all three are
    returned. A play can be graded with no EPA -- CFBD scores almost no
    penalty-wiped play -- and can carry EPA without being graded, as a fumble
    recovery does. Using one as the other is how a coverage problem turns into
    a wrong rate.

    An absent value returns None, never 0.0. Zero EPA allowed reads as a
    perfectly average defence, and absent must not look like average.
    """
    values = pd.to_numeric(frame["_epa"], errors="coerce")
    graded = frame["_graded"]
    successes = int((graded & frame["_derived_success"].fillna(False)).sum())
    epa_plays = int(values.notna().sum())
    epa_total = float(values.sum()) if epa_plays else 0.0
    graded_n = int(graded.sum())

    return {
        "plays": int(len(frame)),
        "graded": graded_n,
        "successes": successes,
        "success_rate": round(successes / graded_n, 4) if graded_n else None,
        "epa_plays": epa_plays,
        "epa_total": round(epa_total, 4) if epa_plays else None,
        "epa_per_play": round(epa_total / epa_plays, 4) if epa_plays else None,
    }


def defence_baseline(
    season_plays: pd.DataFrame,
    opponent_cfbd_name: str,
    cut: str,
    *,
    exclude_garbage: bool = False,
) -> dict:
    """What one defence allowed non-Baylor FBS offences, on one cut.

    Baylor is excluded by offence NAME, not by game, so a hypothetical second
    meeting in the same season is excluded too. Without that the adjustment is
    circular: Baylor's own bad day would make the opponent look better, which
    would then partly excuse Baylor's bad day.

    Offences are filtered to FBS. Every FBS defence plays an FCS body-bag game,
    and leaving it in flatters the baseline and so understates Baylor. The
    parquet is not FBS-only -- 2025 carries 311 defences across 40 conferences,
    including Division II -- so this is a real filter, not a formality.
    """
    frame = season_plays[
        (season_plays["defense"] == opponent_cfbd_name)
        & (season_plays["offense"] != BAYLOR)
        & season_plays["offenseConference"].map(is_fbs)
    ].copy()

    # A Timeout carries the state of the play behind it and a gain of 0. Left
    # in, it is a free failure in every denominator it touches. Penalty rows
    # deliberately stay, matching this repo's existing rule.
    frame = frame[~frame["playType"].map(epa.is_non_play)]

    frame = attach_cut_columns(
        frame,
        play_type_col="playType",
        down_col="down",
        distance_col="distance",
        gain_col="yardsGained",
    )
    frame["_down_for_cut"] = pd.to_numeric(frame["down"], errors="coerce")
    frame["_epa"] = pd.to_numeric(frame["ppa"], errors="coerce")

    if exclude_garbage:
        frame = frame[~flag_garbage(frame)]

    return summarise(apply_cut(frame, cut))


def baylor_cut_frame(
    joined: pd.DataFrame,
    season: int,
    cut: str,
    *,
    exclude_garbage: bool = False,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Baylor's plays for one cut, classified the way the baseline is.

    Every classifying column here comes from CFBD, not the chart, and that is
    the point. The chart records the play CALL and CFBD records the RESULT; 46
    plays are charted `P` and typed `Rush`. A chart-classified Baylor rate
    subtracted from a CFBD-classified baseline would compare two different
    things.

    down and distance are the chart's, and that is not an exception to the
    rule: they are the join key, so on a matched row they equal CFBD's by
    construction.
    """
    frame = joined[joined["season"] == season].copy()
    frame = attach_cut_columns(
        frame,
        play_type_col="cfbd_play_type",
        down_col="down",
        distance_col="distance",
        gain_col="cfbd_yards_gained",
    )
    frame["_down_for_cut"] = pd.to_numeric(frame["down"], errors="coerce")
    frame["_epa"] = pd.to_numeric(frame["epa"], errors="coerce")

    if exclude_garbage:
        frame = frame[~frame["garbage_time"].fillna(False).astype(bool)]

    return apply_cut(frame, cut)


def schedule_strength(
    joined: pd.DataFrame,
    season_plays: pd.DataFrame,
    season: int,
    cut: str,
    *,
    exclude_garbage: bool = False,
    min_sample: int = MIN_SAMPLE,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One row per Baylor game: what Baylor did, and what that defence
    normally allowed.

    This is the descriptive answer on its own. If Baylor's 2025 opponents did
    not allow materially less than its 2024 opponents, opponent adjustment is
    refuted as the explanation before any subtraction is done.

    A baseline thinner than min_sample is blanked, not dropped. The game still
    happened and still counts in the raw figures; only its baseline is
    unusable.
    """
    baylor = baylor_cut_frame(
        joined, season, cut, exclude_garbage=exclude_garbage
    )

    rows = []
    for game_code, game in baylor.groupby("game_code", sort=True):
        code = game["def_team"].dropna().iloc[0]
        # Raises by name on an unmapped code. That is the guard against the
        # bowl-is-week-1 trap: a positional map would misjoin silently.
        name = cfbd.OPPONENT_TO_CFBD[code]

        conference = season_plays.loc[
            season_plays["defense"] == name, "defenseConference"
        ]
        level = opponent_level(conference.iloc[0] if len(conference) else None)

        baseline = defence_baseline(
            season_plays, name, cut, exclude_garbage=exclude_garbage
        )
        summary = summarise(game)

        baseline_epa = baseline["epa_per_play"]
        baseline_sr = baseline["success_rate"]
        if baseline["epa_plays"] < min_sample:
            baseline_epa = None
        if baseline["graded"] < min_sample:
            baseline_sr = None

        rows.append({
            "season": season,
            "cut": cut,
            "game_code": game_code,
            "opponent": code,
            "opponent_cfbd": name,
            "level": level,
            "baylor_plays": summary["plays"],
            "baylor_graded": summary["graded"],
            "baylor_successes": summary["successes"],
            "baylor_epa_plays": summary["epa_plays"],
            "baylor_epa_total": summary["epa_total"],
            "baylor_epa_per_play": summary["epa_per_play"],
            "baylor_success_rate": summary["success_rate"],
            "baseline_plays": baseline["plays"],
            "baseline_graded": baseline["graded"],
            "baseline_epa_plays": baseline["epa_plays"],
            "baseline_epa_per_play": baseline_epa,
            "baseline_success_rate": baseline_sr,
        })

    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def _weighted(values, weights) -> float | None:
    """Play-weighted mean, skipping rows with no value.

    Weighted, not a mean of means: a 90-play game must not weigh what a
    30-play game weighs.
    """
    pairs = [
        (float(value), float(weight))
        for value, weight in zip(values, weights)
        if value is not None and pd.notna(value) and weight
    ]
    if not pairs:
        return None
    total = sum(weight for _, weight in pairs)
    return sum(value * weight for value, weight in pairs) / total


def _ratio(frame: pd.DataFrame, numerator: str, denominator: str) -> float | None:
    total = frame[denominator].sum()
    if not total:
        return None
    return round(frame[numerator].sum() / total, 4)


def _difference(left, right) -> float | None:
    if left is None or right is None:
        return None
    return round(left - right, 4)


def adjusted_table(
    joined: pd.DataFrame,
    plays_by_season: dict,
    cut: str,
    *,
    exclude_garbage: bool = False,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One row per season: raw, raw-FBS-only, baseline, adjusted.

    Three raw columns rather than one, because excluding the FCS game moves
    Baylor's RAW number too. A reader who saw only `adjusted` beside
    REPORT.md's 57.4% would reasonably conclude one document was wrong. The
    step from raw_all_games to raw_fbs_only is schedule COMPOSITION; the step
    from raw_fbs_only to adjusted is opponent QUALITY. Printing only the last
    hides which of the two moved the number.
    """
    rows = []
    for season in sorted(plays_by_season):
        games = schedule_strength(
            joined,
            plays_by_season[season],
            season,
            cut,
            exclude_garbage=exclude_garbage,
        )
        if games.empty:
            continue
        fbs = games[games["level"] == "fbs"]

        baseline_epa = _weighted(
            fbs["baseline_epa_per_play"], fbs["baylor_epa_plays"]
        )
        baseline_sr = _weighted(
            fbs["baseline_success_rate"], fbs["baylor_graded"]
        )
        baseline_epa = round(baseline_epa, 4) if baseline_epa is not None else None
        baseline_sr = round(baseline_sr, 4) if baseline_sr is not None else None

        raw_fbs_epa = _ratio(fbs, "baylor_epa_total", "baylor_epa_plays")
        raw_fbs_sr = _ratio(fbs, "baylor_successes", "baylor_graded")

        rows.append({
            "season": season,
            "cut": cut,
            "games": int(len(games)),
            "games_fbs": int(len(fbs)),
            "plays": int(games["baylor_plays"].sum()),
            "graded": int(games["baylor_graded"].sum()),
            "epa_plays": int(games["baylor_epa_plays"].sum()),
            "raw_all_games_epa": _ratio(
                games, "baylor_epa_total", "baylor_epa_plays"
            ),
            "raw_fbs_only_epa": raw_fbs_epa,
            "schedule_baseline_epa": baseline_epa,
            "adjusted_epa": _difference(raw_fbs_epa, baseline_epa),
            "raw_all_games_sr": _ratio(
                games, "baylor_successes", "baylor_graded"
            ),
            "raw_fbs_only_sr": raw_fbs_sr,
            "schedule_baseline_sr": baseline_sr,
            "adjusted_sr": _difference(raw_fbs_sr, baseline_sr),
        })

    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def reconcile_success(joined: pd.DataFrame) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, dict]:
    """Baylor's charted Efficiency against the 50/70/100 convention.

    CLAUDE.md requires that a re-derived success flag be reconciled against the
    charted one and the disagreement rate reported. Phase 5 re-derives success
    because CFBD has no Efficiency column and no other team is hand-charted, so
    this is that reconciliation.

    It is also a finding in its own right. Nobody in this project has measured
    how far the staff's hand-tagged flag sits from the convention every public
    number uses, and anyone quoting one against the other should know.

    Chart fields on both sides, deliberately, unlike the adjusted tables. The
    question is whether the charted flag agrees with the convention applied to
    the charted gain. Whether the chart agrees with CFBD is a different figure
    and lives in provenance.
    """
    frame = joined[~joined["efficiency"].isin(SUCCESS_RATE_EXCLUDED)].copy()

    frame["_charted"] = frame["efficiency"].eq("Y")
    frame["_derived"] = [
        derive_success(down, distance, gain)
        for down, distance, gain in zip(
            frame["down"], frame["distance"], frame["gain"]
        )
    ]
    frame = frame[frame["_derived"].notna()].copy()
    frame["_derived"] = frame["_derived"].astype(bool)

    crosstab = (
        frame.groupby(["season", "_charted", "_derived"], dropna=False)
        .size()
        .reset_index(name="plays")
        .rename(columns={"_charted": "charted_success",
                         "_derived": "derived_success"})
    )

    compared = int(len(frame))
    agree = int((frame["_charted"] == frame["_derived"]).sum())
    summary = {
        "compared": compared,
        "agreement_rate": round(agree / compared, 4) if compared else None,
        "charted_only": int((frame["_charted"] & ~frame["_derived"]).sum()),
        "derived_only": int((~frame["_charted"] & frame["_derived"]).sum()),
    }
    return crosstab, summary


def classification_audit(season_plays: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Every CFBD play type seen, its count, and how it was classified.

    Published so an unmapped type is visible rather than inferred. A mapping
    that silently stopped covering sacks would still pass every unit test.
    """
    audit = (
        season_plays.groupby("playType", dropna=False)
        .agg(
            plays=("playType", "size"),
            with_epa=("ppa", lambda values: int(values.notna().sum())),
        )
        .reset_index()
    )
    audit["classified_as"] = audit["playType"].map(classify_run_pass)
    audit["is_non_play"] = audit["playType"].map(epa.is_non_play)
    return audit.sort_values("plays", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
